newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers in marathon talks on 1997 fish quotas.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers in marathon talks on 1997 fish quotas.

text.p: European Union fisheries ministers were striving early on Friday, the second day of marathon negotiations, to fix 1997 fish catch quotas.
They were discussing a 32-page compromise proposal from Ireland, the current EU president, which seeks to balance conservation and the economic needs of the fishing industry.
"It's very complex," said an Irish official, adding that negotiations could continue several more hours.
The compromise suggested dropping a proposal by the European Commission to introduce quotas for bluefin tuna in the Mediterranean and Atlantic and for swordfish in the Atlantic.
Italy and Greece had argued that such measures would be unfair as these were the main stocks they exploited.
Proposed measures to restrict sardine fishing off the coasts of Spain and Portugal would also be scrapped.

But EU officials said there were still difficulties over the share-out of quotas under new EU fisheries agreements with the Baltic States following Sweden and Finland's entry into the EU. Germany, Denmark and Finland had major problems with it.

The Dutch and British were also resisting a proposal to slash North Sea sole catches by half to 12,000 tonnes because stocks are at critical levels. The reduction would also affect the associated plaice fishery.
Emergency measures taken in July to protect critically low herring stocks and fixing a 1997 total allowable catch (TAC) of 159,000 tonnes, half the 1995 level, would be extended.
Denmark was unhappy about a proposal to introduce a quota for by-catches of herring by huge vessels hunting sprats for industrial processing into fish meal and oil.
Ministers on Thursday struck a political deal to set up a satellite system to track the mmovement of vessels and curb illegal fishing.
Agreement was reached after Italy came on board having secured a pledge for EU aid to help Italian driftnet fishermen in the Mediterranean to retire or convert to other activities.
But a decision was delayed until April 1997 on controversial plans for further sharp cuts in fishing fleets over the next six years.
